extracted.intended_audience: philosophers of mathematics, cognitive scientists, and mathematically-inclined readers interested in visual cognition of mathematical structures
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and conditions for when a mathematical structure (finite or infinite) can be said to be visually grasped, including use of visual templates, category specifications, recursive/extension rules, and limits of visualization for continuum or high ordinals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Visual template method (isomorphic mapping to a template)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given an instance of a structure, map it isomorphically onto a visual configuration (a template) such as the diagram in Fig. 2.3; the isomorphism can be checked visually.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: the set of nodes structured by ∧, ∨, −, Max and Min is isomorphic to the power set algebra of S; a structured set of this kind is known as a three-atom Boolean algebra and can be checked visually. Practice may allow immediate recognition without carrying out the mapping in thought.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discriminating recognition ability as grasp
rubrics_metrics.description: Grasp of a structure may consist in the ability to tell, given an instance, that it can be mapped isomorphically onto a visual template without actually performing the mapping, provided the ability is discriminating (it would not also lead one to count non-instances as instances).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If this ability is accepted, grasp may be behavioral; alternatively, if that is 'too behaviourist', grasp may be the possession of the cognitive basis underlying that ability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Templates plus uniform visualizable extension rule for structural kinds
rubrics_metrics.description: For a species/kind of finite structures, one should have visual templates for the initial cases together with a uniform rule (a visualizable operation) that produces the 'next' template from a given one.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: discrete linear orderings with endpoints (add a star/line at the right) and finite binary trees (add a 'v' to each terminal point). This combination yields a grasp of the species of structures by providing a template family and extension rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recursive speciﬁcation requirement for visual grasp of a kind
rubrics_metrics.description: A structural kind is amenable to visual grasp when it admits a recursive specification: the smallest two or three structures have visual templates and there is a visualizable operation to obtain the template of the next structure from a given template.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such a kind typically comprises an infinite sequence of often-nested finite structures whose union is an infinite structure; the recursive/specification + templates provide visual awareness of the kind.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between visual images and visual category speciﬁcations
rubrics_metrics.description: Visual images are transient patterns in a visual buffer; visual category speciﬁcations are stored representations (ensembles of feature descriptions) that can generate images when activated and parameterized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kosslyn's architecture: category speciﬁcation activation produces images in a visual buffer; parameters (viewpoint, distance, orientation) continuously vary output. Important for representing infinite structures: category specs can encode 'no right end' whereas images cannot be infinite.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of category speciﬁcations to represent infinite extension
rubrics_metrics.description: Although an infinitely extended visual image is impossible, a category specification can specify features (e.g., a line with no right end) such that imagistic scanning never yields a right-ended image, thereby providing a visual representation of an infinite structure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: the mental number line (marks continuing endlessly to the right) can be represented by a category specification whose dispositions (scanning, answers to structural questions) indicate the intended infinite structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dispositional/answerability criterion for grasp via category specs
rubrics_metrics.description: Grasp of an infinite structured set via a category specification is reflected in dispositions to answer certain structural questions (e.g., given any two marks, must one precede the other? Are intermark spaces uniform?).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These dispositions (yes/no answers) reveal salient structural features (e.g., well-ordering) even though we have no direct access to the internal descriptions of the category specification. Some questions (e.g., 'Is the intermark length more than a centimetre?') may have no answer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combined linguistic/algorithmic and visual constraints to determine unique structure
rubrics_metrics.description: To pick out uniquely the standard model of the natural numbers, one may need both (i) understanding of number-words/numerals and their generative algorithms and (ii) a visual category specification grounded in spatial/temporal constraints (no infinite speeds/durations), together determining well-ordering.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This combined route is offered as an alternative to claiming a prior grasp of the full power set (second-order induction). The visual category spec plus linguistic/numeral algorithms can together secure the uniqueness of the natural number structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations of visual methods for continuum structures (Dedekind-continuity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Visual representations cannot, in general, give knowledge of structures whose crucial feature is Dedekind-continuity (completeness), such as the real unit interval [0,1]; visualizing a line segment fails to reveal that every bounded set has a least upper bound.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reasons: perceptual 'points' have extension and cannot serve as geometrical extensionless points required for the real continuum; line-as-points conception produces paradoxes; visual/tree-branch analogies fail to secure Dedekind-continuity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representability of elements: countability constraint for visual grasp
rubrics_metrics.description: A visual grasp that relies on category specifications is limited by the fact that there are at most countably many category specifications (finite descriptions), but some structures (e.g., the set S of branches corresponding to [0,1]) are uncountable, so most elements cannot be represented and visual grasp fails.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: infinite binary-tree branches—visual images only show finite initial segments shared by infinitely many branches; only finitely many branches may have distinct category specs, so uncountable S resists visual grasp.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concrete visual grasp of some transfinite ordinals (ω, ω2, ω3) via spatial arrays
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain ordinals can be visually grasped by representing them as spatial arrays matching dimensional intuition: ω as an ω-string (horizontal marks), ω2 as an ω-square (vertical stack of ω-strings), ω3 as an ω-cube (layers of ω-squares), giving a category specification that supports claims like termination of decreasing sequences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using the ω-square representation one can see that any decreasing sequence has an uppermost occupied row and a leftmost member in that row, hence terminates; this grounds induction up to ω2. Limitations: this method runs into representational/dimensional limits before ε0.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits to 'grasp at a glance' for complex ordinal possibilities
rubrics_metrics.description: Even where visual array representations yield concrete knowledge (e.g., ω2), one cannot necessarily 'grasp at a glance all the structural possibilities' for decreasing sequences (there are sequences with elements arbitrarily far to the right), so some claims of immediate evidential grasp are overstated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gödel's remark about recursion up to ε0 is discussed: while recursion/induction for some ordinals can be made 'immediately evident' via visual methods, this fails for larger ordinals (e.g., ε0) because the needed steps are too small and too numerous to be captured by a visualizable transition.
